headline: Control, Memory, and Identity Across Emerging Technical Systems
narrative_html:
Control, Memory, and Identity Across Emerging Technical Systems

A recurring lesson in complex systems is that capable components do not guarantee a reliable whole. Whether the components are AI agents, formal definitions, image elements, physical controllers, or specialized cells, success often depends on preserving the right state, constraints, and identity over time.

Why Smarter Agents Cannot Recover Missing Shared State

The global coherence problem arises when every agent makes a defensible decision from its own view, yet the combined result is invalid. The paper’s abstract argues that this is fundamentally an information problem rather than merely a deficit in reasoning. If two possible worlds look identical to an agent but require incompatible actions, no amount of deliberation can reveal which world is real. More messages, specialized roles, repeated samples, or a stronger model help only if they introduce the missing distinction.

The stated Observation-Aliasing Impossibility Theorem makes that boundary precise: a policy can guarantee a valid action only when all worlds consistent with the same observation have at least one admissible action in common. If there are k indistinguishable worlds whose valid action sets are pairwise disjoint, even the best randomized policy has worst-case success of only 1/k. This formalizes a familiar operational failure. An agent asked whether it may spend the remaining budget cannot answer reliably if it cannot see purchases committed by other agents. Its local reasoning may be flawless while its premise about the shared state is obsolete.

The proposed runtime separates model proposals from authoritative execution. Its formal vocabulary includes a topology for overlapping scopes, structures for state-changing and reversible operations, a sheaf-like test for whether local views can be combined into one consistent world, and a minimal history retaining only distinctions that change future legal actions. The practical core is simpler than this mathematical apparatus: the harness, not the language model, owns shared state and decides whether an action may commit.

The reported studies support that operational point. A controlled revision task allegedly fell from 40 correct decisions out of 40 to roughly chance performance, 12 to 17 out of 40, when the decisive event was hidden; restoring one authoritative fact returned performance to 40 out of 40. On TeamBench, ordinary teams exceeded a shared budget in all five runs, a visible live count still left four violations, and commit-time enforcement eliminated them. A telecommunications experiment reports a score of 0.07 for current-state checks after silent reverts versus 1.00 for the harness. These are striking results, although the abstract alone does not expose benchmark design or statistical robustness. The deepest contribution is the boundary it draws: use models to propose and interpret, but put concurrency, permissions, invariants, and commits in a system that actually possesses the relevant state.

What a Small Lean Proof Teaches Software Engineers

The worked example begins with a standard automata-theory exercise. Each input symbol is a vertical column of three bits, so a word encodes three binary numbers. The language contains exactly those words for which the bottom row is the sum of the top two. To prove that this language is regular, one must show that a deterministic finite automaton with fixed memory can recognize it, no matter how long the numbers become.

Ordinary binary addition suggests the finite state: when processing one column, the machine needs to remember only the carry. The difficulty is direction. The input presents the most significant bits first, while manual addition naturally proceeds from the least significant bit. The solution therefore constructs an adder automaton for the reversed language. It reads low-order columns first, verifies each output bit using the two input bits and incoming carry, and records the outgoing carry in its state. Once that reversed language is recognized by a DFA, closure of regular languages under reversal establishes that the original language is regular.

The Lean formalization turns that compact argument into explicit definitions and proof obligations. According to the available contents, it specifies the language and automaton, proves an invariant over an automaton run by induction, splits a run into its first transition and remaining transitions, and handles the least-significant-bit arithmetic needed for the inductive step. It then connects acceptance by the adder DFA to membership in the reversed language and finally invokes regular-language closure to recover the original result.

For software engineers, the value is not the theorem itself but the exposure of everything an informal proof leaves implicit. One must align the representation of bit strings, numerical interpretation, reversal, transition execution, carry arithmetic, and library definitions closely enough that every step type-checks. That resembles verification work: the hard part is often discovering the invariant and choosing definitions that make the desired correspondence expressible. The extract ends before the full proof, so its exact Lean code and proof complexity cannot be assessed here, but the example is well chosen. It is small enough to understand completely while still demonstrating why formal proof is more than writing an ordinary argument in stricter syntax.

An Irrigation Agent That Is Not Allowed to Rewrite Physics

Irrigation is a demanding test for an AI agent because a decision made today changes the soil conditions under which tomorrow’s decision will be made. Watering too little can stress a crop; watering too much wastes water and may create other agronomic costs. Feedback unfolds over a season, and a bad action cannot simply be erased by resetting an episodic benchmark.

Mimir addresses this through two repair loops. In the fast loop, the language model does not directly operate the irrigation system. It produces a structured proposal, which a deterministic simulator evaluates against soil-water dynamics. The system can numerically check and revise that proposal before a bounded deterministic mechanism selects an executable action. In the slow loop, repeated failures are distilled into persistent contextual principles that influence later proposals. Crucially, this learning process cannot alter the physical model, evaluator, or execution constraints.

The authors report that, under a common retrospective evaluator spanning multiple sites, crops, and years, Mimir achieved the lowest aggregate control cost among the compared methods and used about 51 percent less irrigation than replaying historical schedules. Removing forward simulation, verified revision, or persistent context raised cost. Increasing model size or changing to a supposedly stronger family did not produce a monotonic improvement, suggesting that system architecture mattered more than raw language-model scale in this setting.

The result is practically important if it survives prospective field deployment. It illustrates a credible division of labor: an LLM can interpret context, propose strategies, and retain lessons, while numerical models enforce physical reality and retain actuator authority. But the abstract reports retrospective evaluation, not live agricultural operation, and does not reveal how accurately the simulator represents weather uncertainty, soil heterogeneity, sensor errors, or crop response. Those details determine whether the reported water savings transfer to farms. The architecture is nevertheless more convincing than an unconstrained autonomous agent because its adaptation occurs inside immutable safety and physics boundaries.

FLUX 3 Pitches Images as Structured, Editable Compositions

The FLUX 3 Image page presents an image system aimed at more than one-shot text-to-image generation. Its most distinctive advertised interface lets a user specify elements with bounding boxes, identifiers, and descriptions. In the supplied festival example, separate boxes place a title, coastal town, concrete dome, swimmers, and beach crowd. This converts composition from a vague phrase in a prompt into an explicit spatial plan.

The page also claims strong ordinary prompt following, the ability to combine as many as ten reference images, simultaneous localized edits that leave unrelated content unchanged, and native 2K and 4K output. An element table appears to expose a scene in a form that software can inspect or manipulate. The product is also described as designed for agents, which likely means an automated system can issue structured layout and editing instructions rather than relying exclusively on natural-language prompting.

If the claims hold under difficult tests, the bounding-box and element model is more consequential than another incremental gain in visual polish. Production workflows need repeatability: art directors want to move one subject, recolor two objects, preserve a face, or keep typography in a reserved region without regenerating the entire scene. A structured interface could also make image generation easier to integrate into design tools and automated pipelines.

The extract is promotional and supplies no benchmark results, latency, pricing, failure analysis, or independent comparisons. Terms such as “pixel perfect” and “exactly” should therefore be read as marketing claims rather than established performance guarantees. The real tests would include crowded scenes, overlapping boxes, readable text, identity preservation across edits, and whether untouched pixels or merely the broad appearance remain stable. The interface direction is promising, but the evidence available here cannot establish its reliability.

Catching Policy Drift That Averages Away

Reinforcement-learning post-training often generates responses with one policy configuration and trains on them after the policy or inference stack has changed. The resulting samples are off-policy: token probabilities under the training policy no longer match those under the policy that produced the response. Excessive mismatch can make optimization unstable or misleading, so systems may mask out responses whose probability ratios have drifted too far.

A common response-level test averages signed token log-ratios, equivalently using a length-normalized geometric mean of probability ratios. The weakness is cancellation. If the new policy makes some sampled tokens much more likely and others much less likely, positive and negative log-ratios can average close to zero. The response then appears safely on-policy even though its token-level distribution has shifted substantially in both directions.

Cancellation-Aware Response Masking changes the statistic by taking the absolute value of every token log-ratio before averaging. Opposing changes can no longer hide one another. The authors also claim a theorem for accepted responses that jointly bounds how many sampled-token ratios may lie outside a specified band and how far, on average, the outlying log-ratios extend beyond that band. This gives the threshold a more direct interpretation than a signed aggregate.

The reported gains are up to 3.13 percentage points on a mean-at-16 aggregate covering several AIME and BeyondAIME mathematical evaluations, and 2.88 points in average pass-at-1 across four coding benchmarks relative to the strongest evaluated baseline. Without the full paper, it is unclear how sensitive those improvements are to thresholds, training recipes, or compute. Conceptually, however, the fix is clean and plausible. It targets a specific statistical blind spot rather than adding a complex training subsystem, making it the kind of incremental technique that could have broad practical value if replicated.

Aging as the Erosion of Cellular Identity

The article describes a model of aging that complements accumulated molecular damage with a failure of cells to preserve what kind of cells they are. Most cells contain nearly the same DNA, but a neuron, liver cell, and epithelial cell use that genome differently because their chromatin organization, histone state, DNA methylation, and other epigenetic features make different genes accessible. Cellular identity therefore depends not just on genetic sequence but on a durable regulatory architecture.

The proposed framework divides regulation into three timescales. A fast layer responds to acute stress over minutes or hours through factors such as AP-1. An intermediate layer supports state changes over days or weeks, including activation for wound healing followed by a return to baseline. A slow chromatin layer establishes the hard boundaries that stabilize a cell’s long-term identity. Using Waddington’s landscape metaphor, a young differentiated cell lies in a deep valley that resists displacement; with aging, that valley becomes shallower, making the cell’s state less stable.

The account assigns a central role to the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2, or PRC2, in maintaining this landscape. It further claims that PRC2-associated low-methylated regions help explain what epigenetic clocks measure. Chronic inflammation may overwhelm short-term responses and disrupt the slower architecture, leaving persistent chromatin changes even after the inflammation subsides. The resulting loss of constraint can push specialized cells toward mesenchymal-like states associated with extracellular-matrix deposition, fibrosis, and inflammation. A cited Cell study reportedly finds this mesenchymal drift across 46 tissue types and associates it with disease progression and poor outcomes.

This is an appealing synthesis because it connects epigenetic aging, inflammation, fibrosis, and cancer-like loss of identity. It should not, however, be reduced to the claim that damage no longer matters. The article itself acknowledges uncertainty about the relative contributions and interdependence of damage and identity loss. Inflammation or molecular damage could erode chromatin control, while destabilized identity could in turn worsen inflammation and tissue dysfunction. Cause and consequence may form a feedback loop rather than two competing explanations.

The suggested interventions vary enormously in maturity. Caloric restriction may help preserve regulatory architecture, but primate results have been inconsistent and sustained restriction in people is difficult. Partial reprogramming with Yamanaka factors seeks to restore a younger epigenetic state without erasing identity completely; animal and cell findings are intriguing, but full reprogramming can produce pluripotency and cancer risk. An OSK approach excluding c-Myc is reportedly being tested by direct eye injection for severe optic-nerve damage. Lithium is also discussed through pathways involving GSK3 beta, neuronal identity, and tau phosphorylation, but mechanistic plausibility is not clinical proof that lithium prevents Alzheimer’s disease. The identity model is scientifically important because it suggests aging may be partly reversible, yet safe organism-wide rejuvenation remains highly uncertain.

Teaching a VR Generator the User’s Spatial Logic

Generative VR authoring becomes tedious when a system forgets a user’s preferences after every session. Repeatedly correcting furniture placement or room organization is not only inefficient but physically tiring in an immersive interface. SPHERE is designed to retain those corrections as persistent spatial preferences rather than treating every generated scene as a fresh request.

The framework learns from both speech and controller-based edits. Instead of storing only superficial choices such as favored colors or object types, it converts edits into hierarchical constraints. Local constraints can represent functional relations among nearby objects, while global constraints capture broader topology and room organization. That distinction matters: a preference such as keeping a chair near a desk is different from a preference about circulation paths, sight lines, or how functional zones relate across an entire room.

A human-in-the-loop reinforcement-learning component updates retrieval policies using the scenes users ultimately accept after editing. In effect, the final scene becomes evidence about which remembered preferences should be retrieved for a later task. The authors report a mixed-design study with 42 participants and an offline ablation, with reductions in corrective edits and physical demand. They also claim that the hierarchical representation avoids overfitting to shallow object-level traits and produces layouts that remain geometrically coherent.

The practical contribution is persistent personalization with an intermediate constraint layer that users and software can potentially govern. Pure end-to-end adaptation risks learning incidental correlations, whereas explicit spatial relations offer a clearer target for inspection and correction. The abstract does not provide effect sizes, task duration, or details about the diversity of rooms and participants, so the strength and generality of the user-study result cannot be judged. Still, learning demonstrated spatial logic rather than merely preferred objects is the right conceptual move for serious design assistance.

Generating Mobility in Cities With No Local Trajectory Data

Synthetic mobility models usually learn where people travel from observed trajectories in the city where the model will be deployed. That excludes cities with no accessible movement records, even when their maps and points of interest are public. Nomad tackles the stricter case in which the target city supplies only point-of-interest coordinates and categories, with no local trajectories or trajectory-derived statistics available for training, model selection, or generation.

The key factorization separates movement behavior from city-specific destinations. Rather than learning that a person should next visit a particular named place or coordinate, the model learns relative transitions: given a history and the semantic context of the current place, what kind of place tends to follow, how far away it tends to be, and how much time tends to elapse. A history-conditioned flow-matching model learns this transition prior from source cities.

At inference time, those abstract transitions must be grounded in the target city’s actual geography. Nomad uses a behavior graph and an exploration-return walk to map sampled intentions onto available target points of interest. The exploration-return mechanism reflects the broad pattern that people alternate between visiting new places and returning to familiar ones. This does not assume that the entire mobility distribution is invariant across cities; it tests whether a more limited representation of relative movement can transfer.

Across ten cities and 14 transfer settings, the authors report about a 15 percent average error reduction in distributional fidelity and roughly a 3 percent improvement in downstream utility over the best baseline for each metric. The disparity is informative: synthetic trajectories can look more statistically realistic without producing equally large gains in applications that consume them. More importantly, public POI maps omit many determinants of real travel, including transit quality, working hours, income, accessibility, congestion, and local culture. Nomad’s factorization is a meaningful advance for data-scarce settings, but generated trajectories should not be mistaken for observed local behavior, especially in policy decisions where demographic bias and neighborhood-level errors matter.

item.title: Global Coherence: When Every Agent Is Right and the Team Is Still Wrong - A Local-to-Global Semantic Foundation for Multi-Agent Collaboration
item.summary:
AI agents can each make locally valid decisions yet jointly produce an invalid result. We call this the global coherence problem: a failure of shared state, not merely of model intelligence.
  Our Observation-Aliasing Impossibility Theorem gives the exact boundary. A policy can guarantee a valid action exactly when all worlds producing the same observation share an admissible action. If k indistinguishable worlds require pairwise-disjoint actions, the best randomized worst-case success is 1/k; more reasoning, roles, messages, or samples cannot recover the missing distinction. A stronger model can reason better within its context, but it cannot see beyond it.
  We then give local-to-global runtime semantics X = (H, C, G, F; D): topology H records overlapping scopes; category C governs state-changing actions; groupoid G retains reversible translations; sheaf F tests whether local views glue into one world; and minimal history D keeps only distinctions that alter legal futures. Models propose; the harness owns shared state and governs commit.
  Nine studies test both the failure and its boundary. On a controlled revision benchmark, the same frontier model scores 40/40 when the deciding event is visible; when it is hidden, tested arms score 12--17/40, consistent with chance (1/3); restoring one authoritative fact returns 40/40. The counterintuitive conclusion is that local intelligence cannot substitute for missing global state.

items.context: In multi-agent systems, agents may act on different or incomplete views of a shared situation, so individually valid decisions can conflict when combined. The abstract describes this as a shared-state and coordination problem, and proposes runtime mechanisms for checking whether local views agree before actions are committed. These are the source’s framing and proposed semantics; its specific theorem and benchmark results are claims reported in the abstract, not general background facts.
items.why: The abstract is worth reading for its precise account of when missing information limits coordination: it claims that agents cannot reliably distinguish worlds that look identical to them but require incompatible actions. It also reports tests where commit enforcement prevented budget violations and a harness handled silent reverts better than current-state checks, while matching a conventional solver when that solver had the complete relevant state. These examples make the proposed distinction between better reasoning and better shared-state management concrete.

item.title: Anatomy of a Lean proof for software engineers
item.summary: [Contents]IntroBackground: DFAs & Regular LanguagesDeterministic Finite Automaton (DFA)Regular LanguagesThe ProblemThe SolutionAdder ArithmeticAdder DFAExample 1Example 2The Lean ProofThe SpecificationThe ImplementationHow Proofs WorkThe ProofRun InvariantRun Invariant ProofBase CaseInductive StepSplitting the RunFirst Step AddsLeast Significant Bit SplitPutting It TogetherBRB^{\mathcal{R}} Is RegularAdder DFA Accepts BRB^{\mathcal{R}}From Acceptance to RegularityBB Is RegularOutroIntroI recently worked through a problem from a theory of computation textbook that asked me to prove a property of a language using finite automata. The informal proof is a simple constructive proof where you build an automaton and show that it recognizes the language. This is kind of similar to program verification, so I thought it’d be interesting to see what it takes to formalize the proof. Lean is a good choice for this, because its Mathlib has all the theorems for the problem.After finishing the formal proof, I decided to write it up, because I think it provides software engineers with good insight into what it takes to formally prove properties of a system.I tried to make this post accessible. If you’re comfortable with a modern statically typed programming language (such as TypeScript or Rust), binary arithmetic, basic propositional logic, and inductive proofs, you should be able to follow along.Background: DFAs & Regular LanguagesFeel free to skip to the next section if you’re comfortable with DFAs and regular languages.Finite automata provide a theoretical model of computation with fixed memory. Besides theory, finite automata also have important practical applications. For example, finite automata are relevant for parsers and regular expressions, where a bug once took a significant portion of the internet down.Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA)A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) is a machine with a fixed, finite set of states that reads its input one symbol at a time, left to right. With each symbol, it updates its state using a deterministic transition function. After the last symbol, the machine either sits in an accepting state (input is accepted) or not (input is rejected).If you’ve ever written a simple regular expression like -?[0-9]+, then you’ve constructed a DFA. This regex matches integer literals like 12 and -123 and the corresponding DFA looks like this (the arrows are annotated with the symbols that lead to the next state):DFA for a decimal integer literal, including the dead statestartsigndigitsdead-0-90-90-9otherotherotheranyThis DFA has four states:Start: this is where we start before processing the first character. Since the start state is not an accepting state, we reject the empty string.Sign: we move to the sign state when we encounter the - character in the start state. We can skip the sign state and jump directly to digits from start, since the sign character is optional (-?). If we’re in this state at the end of the string, then we reject the string.Digits: we move from start or sign to digits when we encounter a digit character ([0-9]). If we’re in the digits state and encounter a digit character again, then we stay in the digits state. The digits state is the only accepting state of the DFA. If we’re in this state after we’ve processed the input string, then the DFA accepts the string.Dead: we get into this state if we encounter any other character than a digit (unless it’s a negative sign at the start). If we’re in the dead state at the end of the string, then the DFA rejects the string. Once we’re in the dead state, we stay in it, so the dead state in this DFA is a sink.The set of input symbols to the machine is defined by the set Σ\Sigma. In our regex example, Σ={−,0,1,2,…,9}\Sigma = \left\{-, 0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9\right\}.Regular LanguagesA language is just a set of strings, also called words, and a language is called regular if some DFA accepts exactly the strings in it. Recognizing regular languages is the class of decision problems solvable with an amount of memory that does not grow with the input.Regular languages have useful closure properties: the union and intersection of two regular languages are regular, and so are the complement and (important for us) the reversal of a regular language.The standard way to prove that a language is regular is to build a DFA and show that it accepts exactly that language.We can describe a language AA with set-builder notation:A={ w∈Σ∗∣P(w) }A = \bigl\{\, w \in \Sigma^{*} \bigm| P(w) \,\bigr\}Σ∗\Sigma^{*} means the set of strings that are created by all possible concatenations of symbols in Σ\Sigma and P(w)P(w) is the condition that a string ww must satisfy to be in the language.Let’s apply this notation to our regex example: -?[0-9]+. Then Σ∗\Sigma^{*} contains strings like "", "123", "-111", "2-625-", etc. and P(w)P(w) can be defined as “ww is not empty and contains no negative sign, except that its first character may be a negative sign if ww has at least two characters”.The ProblemThe problem that we’re going to solve is from the Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed. by Michael Sipser:1.32 LetΣ3={[000],[001],[010],…,[111]}.\Sigma_3 = \left\{ \begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}0\\1\\0\end{bmatrix}, \ldots, \begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{bmatrix} \right\}.Σ3\Sigma_3 is the set of all height-3 columns of 0s and 1s, so a string over Σ3\Sigma_3 determines three rows of bits. Reading each row as a binary number, defineB={ w∈Σ3∗∣P(w) }B = \bigl\{\, w \in \Sigma_3^{*} \bigm| P(w) \,\bigr\}where P(w)P(w) is the proposition that the bottom row of ww equals the sum of the top two rows.Show that BB is regular. (Hint: it is easier to work with BRB^{\mathcal{R}}.)The problem defines an unusual alphabet. Instead of regular characters like [a-z], the alphabet is made up of columns of three bits. So instead of a language that consists of strings like "apple", "banana", etc., the language consists of two-dimensional bit strings like011 001 100 where the first column is the first “character” and so on.The rule to decide whether a string is in the language is to add the first two rows of the string and check whether they match the third.For example, the following string is in the language:011 # x row: first addend is 3 in decimal 001 # y row: second addend is 1 in decimal 100 # z row: sum is 4 which is equal to 3 + 1 But the following string is not in the language:01 # x row: first addend is 1 in decimal 00 # y row: second addend is 0 11 # z row: sum is 3 which is not equal to 1 + 0 While a language like this may look weird at first, it’s actually easy to recognize: we just need to check the equationx+y=z x + y = zto determine whether a string is in the language. The challenge is that we need to do this with a fixed amount of memory for arbitrarily long strings.The SolutionThe trick is to remember how you add numbers by hand: you work from the least significant digit to the most significant. The only thing you carry from one column to the next is the carry.But a DFA reads left to right, and the problem presents the numbers most significant bit first. So we don’t recognize BB directly. Instead we build a DFA to recognize its reversal BRB^{\mathcal{R}}, which consists of the strings of BB written backwards, so the machine sees the least significant column first.If we can build a DFA to recognize BRB^{\mathcal{R}}, then we can conclude that BRB^{\mathcal{R}} is a regular language. items.context: A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) reads symbols one at a time, updates among finitely many states, and accepts or rejects at the end; a language is regular when some DFA accepts exactly its strings. The source applies these ideas to strings of three-bit columns encoding two addends and their sum. Since addition is easiest from least significant bit to most significant, it considers the reversed language, then uses the general closure of regular languages under reversal. These are background concepts; the source’s particular contribution is to formalize this construction and its proof in Lean.
items.why: The article offers a worked example of turning an informal, constructive automata argument into a Lean proof, with sections on the specification, implementation, and a run invariant proved by base case and inductive step. Its focus on a concrete arithmetic example may help software engineers see how formal proofs connect a system’s behavior to a stated property.

item.title: Mimir: Physics-Grounded LLM Agents for Long-Horizon Irrigation Control
item.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly combine reasoning, tool use, and action, but most evidence comes from episodic tasks with relatively immediate feedback and reset failures. Long-running physical control operates in a different regime: actions alter future states, errors compound across decisions, and an agent must improve from experience without being allowed to rewrite the physical rules that make execution safe. We study this regime through irrigation, where daily decisions interact with soil-water dynamics over entire growing seasons. We present Mimir, a physics-grounded LLM agent organized around two repair timescales. At the fast timescale, a structured physical interface and deterministic simulator turn an LLM output into a proposal that we numerically check, revise, and subject to bounded deterministic action selection before execution. At the slow timescale, recurrent failure patterns are consolidated into persistent contextual principles that condition future proposals, while the physical model, evaluator, and execution constraints remain immutable. Under a common retrospective evaluator across multiple sites, crops, and years, Mimir attains the lowest reported aggregate control cost among the evaluated references and uses about 51% less irrigation than the historical schedule replay. The ablation study show higher control cost when forward simulation, verified revision, or persistent context is removed; model-scale and model-family studies show no monotonic gain from increasing LLM size. The resulting lesson show that persistent physical agents can combine semantic reasoning with bounded, evidence-driven self-improvement while reserving physical truth and actuator authority for explicit numerical mechanisms.

items.context: Long-horizon physical control differs from one-off tasks because actions change future system states and mistakes can accumulate. In irrigation, daily choices interact with soil-water dynamics over a growing season. The abstract describes an agent whose language-model proposals are checked and bounded by a numerical simulator; these are the source’s design choices, not general requirements for every control system.
items.why: The abstract reports lower aggregate control cost than the evaluated references and about 51% less irrigation than replaying historical schedules, under a shared retrospective evaluator across sites, crops, and years. Its ablations also report higher costs when key components are removed, making the work relevant to readers interested in how simulation, verification, and persistent learning might support safer long-running agents.

items.context: Text-to-image systems create images from written prompts, while image-editing systems modify selected parts of an existing image. Bounding boxes can specify where elements should appear or which regions to edit, and reference images can guide a generated composition. This post presents FLUX 3 Image as supporting these workflows, including high-resolution output; those are claims in the supplied extract, not independently verified findings.

It may help readers assess the tool’s stated capabilities, though the partial post does not provide independent performance evidence.

item.title: CARM: Cancellation-Aware Response Masking for LLM Reinforcement Learning
item.summary: Recent years have witnessed the rapid adoption of reinforcement learning (RL) in large language model (LLM) post-training, with substantial gains in mathematical reasoning and code generation. In practical systems, however, policy updates and differences between rollout and training engines can make sampled responses off-policy. Sequence-level masking addresses this mismatch by deciding whether an entire response should contribute to optimization. A common masking rule uses the length-normalized geometric mean of sampled token probability ratios. Its signed log-ratios can cancel across positions, concealing substantial bidirectional policy drift. We propose \emph{Cancellation-Aware Response Masking} (CARM), a sequence-level mask that takes the absolute value of each token log-ratio before averaging, preventing opposing probability changes from canceling. We prove that accepted responses satisfy a joint bound on the fraction of sampled-token ratios outside a prescribed band and their mean log-distance beyond its boundaries. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that CARM improves mean@16 averaged over AIME 2024/2025/2026 and BeyondAIME by up to $3.13$ percentage points over geometric-mean masking, and increases average pass@1 across four code benchmarks by $2.88$ points over the strongest evaluated baseline. These findings support CARM as a theoretically grounded and effective method for response-level off-policy control in LLM reinforcement learning.

items.context: In LLM reinforcement learning, a model is updated using sampled responses, but differences between the system that generates those responses and the one used for training can make them off-policy. Sequence-level masking decides whether a whole response contributes to an update. The abstract says a common rule averages token probability ratios geometrically; CARM instead averages the absolute token log-ratios so opposing changes cannot cancel. These are the source’s method description and claims, rather than general background facts about all RL systems.
items.why: The abstract presents both a theoretical result—a joint bound on token-ratio deviations for accepted responses—and benchmark results: improvements over geometric-mean masking on mathematical reasoning and over the strongest evaluated baseline on code generation. It may be useful to readers interested in how response-level masking can address policy drift in LLM reinforcement learning; these results are reported in the abstract, not independently assessed here.

item.title: Loss of cell identity drives human aging: Two new papers
item.summary: Two new papers, one published today in Nature by Vadim Gladyshev and colleagues at Harvard, and a recent one in Cell by Juan Carlos Izpisua Belmonte and his team at Altos Labs, have provided a new model for the biology of aging, and what might be done to reverse it. Until recently we accepted that aging of cells was due to “wear and tear” like rusting out a car. The idea that accumulated damage is the principal pathway for cell aging is now complemented by the loss of cell identity model. We don’t know the relative contribution or interdependence of these 2 models in the aging process. Two different models for why cells age, made with ChatGPT In this edition of Ground Truths I’m going to explain the loss of cell identity, how it leads to mesenchymal drift (fibrous scarring and inflammation), and how this new model furthers the potential to intervene in the aging process. Share Ground TruthsIn embryonic and early development, our cells establish an identity. It’s locked in throughout our lives, except when it’s lost during the aging process. Although the DNA of every cell of our body is the same (or very close, if interested, see), the epigenetic structure, that includes methylation side chains, histones, nucleosomes and chromatin, is 3-dimensional and differs as a function of cell type. This is happening in the cell’s “mission control,” the nucleus. The epigenetic structure is the bedrock for our cell-specific identity.There’s a 3-tier regulatory “grammar” that maintains the cell identity as shown below.(Figure from the Nature paper). The fast layer responds to acute stress in a matter of minutes to hours and relies on production of transcription factors, like AP-1. The intermediate layer takes days to weeks to respond, going through cell state transitions such as activating a cell to promote healing and return to its basal state. The key is the slow layer, he one that locks and insulates the cell identity, the hard boundary, relying on chromatin architecture.That gets us to Waddington’s epigenetic landscape model for how cells differentiate or de-differentiate, a model that has held up well from Conrad Waddington in 1957! A cell sitting down in the valley (Figure below, culled together from the Nature paper) represents a distinct specialized cell. The deep slope indicates the robustness, also called canalization, accompanied by a deep basin, maintains the identity of the cell, promotes its stability. The differentiated cell is “staying in its lane” in the landscape model and is constrained from sliding out, shifting identity. But with aging, the valleys lose their slope, the basin becomes shallow, there is loss of epigenetic constraints, and there is instability of cell identity. That sets up drift of cell identity, or what can be regarded as mesenchymal drift.Over the lifespan, as shown on the right side of the Figure below, after peak maturation with the specialized cells (brain, liver heart,kidney, etc) fully and irrevocably differentiated (peak functional state below), the valleys are losing slope and the basins are progressively getting shallower, known as decanalization. The problem is that there is no evolutionary pressure to keep the grooves, valleys and basin in their youthful state, because the “selection shadow” is a post-reproductive trajectory.The polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) can be seen as the sculptor of this epigenetic landscape, the molecular machinery that shapes the grooves, valleys, and basin. It establishes the hard boundary, the deep epigenetic constraints for cell identity.Epigenetic clocks are remarkably informative across 348 mammalian species, including humans, for predicting maximal lifespan and life history, but we didn’t know what they are actually measuring. It turns out it’s PRC2, the pace of slow layer erosion! (Figure below, to be precise, it’s the PRC2 low-methylated regions).PRC2 comes into play when there is chronic inflammation overriding the fast layer capacity to respond and blocking PRC2, leading to erosion of the Waddington landscape, promoting cell identity loss. Even after chronic inflammation is resolved, there are epigenetic changes in chromatin that can persist. This loss of epigenetic grammar can also be the foundation for cancer cells. Eventual erosion of the slow layer essentially portends architectural collapse of the Waddington landscape.Schematic of PRC2, what epigenetic clocks are capturing. Made with Google NotebookThe mesenchymal state, as schematically shown below, in this example for an epithelial cell representative of all differentiated, specialized cells. Schematic of drift, made with Google NotebookNow we turn to the Cell paper which goes deep on the mesenchymal drift. This denotes the change of cells to a mesenchymal state, resembling fibroblasts, engendering fibrous scar, laying down extracellular matrix, like mushy putty. It has been verified in 46 tissue types and is part and parcel of disease progression and poor outcomes, as shown below (Figure from the Cell paper). If you are checking for the tie-in between mesenchymal drift and age-related diseases, you’ll find them here, from atherosclerosis, to age-related macular degeneration, to Alzheimer’s disease. Now that we have an enhanced understanding of the process, which has a positive feedback loop as depicted below, fibroblast sthat are activating in turn activating more fibroblasts to induce scarring (Figure from the Cell paper), how can we intervene to freeze the drift, avoid the slow layer erosion, and preserve the Waddington landscape, keeping cells locked in their designated identity? Or, even more ambitious, actually turn back the loss of erosion that has occurred?Caloric restriction (CR), with its attendant reduced acetyl CoA, and reduced PRC2 methylation, promotes the preservation of slow layer architecture, conceptually freezing the drift. CR has been shown to promote lifespan in mammalian species but the results in non-human primates have been inconsistent, and the magnitude and duration of caloric restriction likely required in people is impractical. Still there may be, theoretically, a partial effect of avoidance of high caloric intake to help prevent erosion.The use of the Yamanaka stem cell factors is the far-reaching intervention—rejuvenating cells— that has attracted the most attention and huge investment by biotech companies. But it’s tricky because it requires a brief exposure to the 4 transcription factors, OSKM (Oct-4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc), called “partial” epigenetic reprogramming, in order to avoid full reprogramming, which erases their memory and turns cells into pluripotent stem cells. That carries an increased risk for cancer. But partial reprogramming using short bursts, rejuvenation is seen, with restoration of cell identity in aged human fibroblasts (even from age 96 years) and in animal models. The slow layer is restored, the PRC2 domains are re-established, and the mesenchymal drift is actively reversed. An alternative to short exposure for partial reprogramming is the use of 3 transcription factors OSK (no c-Myc) which is being tested in a pilot study of patients with severe optic nerve damage using direct eye injection.The Nature paper also gets into lithium as an intervention for maintaining neuron identity by interfering with the pathway of slow layer failure. I won’t get into the details of all the mediators (β-catenin, EDH2-USP7, KDM1A, REST, GSK3β, etc) but lithium’s impact on GSK3β blocks tau phosphorylation in experimental models. Lithium orotate has been raised as a candidate for preventing Alzheimer’s, as I’ve previously written about, and this mechanism may be operative. There continues to be extraordinary progress in the science of aging. Beyond the old dogma that this is just the cumulative outgrowth of cell mutations and damage, we now understand the epigenetic basis: the loss of cell identity serves as both a driver and result of the aging process. items.context: Cell identity is the specialized state of a cell, maintained in part by epigenetic regulation of how DNA is organized and used; Waddington’s landscape is a metaphor for how stable or changeable cell states can be. The source presents loss of this stability as a model that complements the familiar idea of aging through accumulated cellular damage. It reports that the papers it discusses link age-related epigenetic changes with drift toward mesenchymal, scar-forming cell states, while noting that the models’ relative contributions remain unknown.
items.why: The material offers a readable synthesis of two recent papers, connecting proposed mechanisms of cell aging to tissue scarring and possible interventions such as partial epigenetic reprogramming. It also distinguishes promising experimental results from unresolved questions, including the risks of reprogramming and the uncertain relevance of some approaches to people.

item.title: SPHERE: Adaptive VR Indoor Scene Generation via LLM-Enhanced Spatial Preference Learning and Human-in-the-Loop RL
item.summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) advance 3D indoor scene synthesis, current pipelines fail to retain user-specific preferences across sessions, making immersive authoring a repetitive and physically fatiguing process. We present SPHERE, an adaptive VR generation framework that transforms isolated synthesis into continuous human-AI co-creation. SPHERE extracts persistent spatial preferences from natural multimodal interactions (speech and controller edits). To ensure geometric resilience against spatial distortions, it abstracts these raw edits into hierarchical constraints modeling both local functional and global topological contexts. Furthermore, a human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning mechanism dynamically updates retrieval policies based on the user's final edited scenes. A mixed-design user study ($N=42$) and an offline ablation demonstrate that SPHERE significantly reduces corrective edits and physical demand, preventing bias toward shallow object-level traits to yield geometrically resilient, profile-aligned layouts. Ultimately, SPHERE demonstrates how capturing demonstrated spatial logic enables controlled spatial adaptation, establishing a reliable, governed human-AI collaboration framework for immersive authoring. Project page and source code will be available at: https://github.com/hyeonmin11/SPHERE

items.context: VR indoor scene generation uses software to create room layouts for immersive environments. In general, language models can help synthesize scenes, while speech and controller edits provide ways for users to express preferences. The abstract describes SPHERE as carrying preferences across sessions by representing edits as hierarchical constraints—covering local functional and global topological relationships—and updating retrieval policies through human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning. These are the paper’s proposed methods, not general guarantees about such systems.
items.why: The abstract may interest readers exploring adaptive creative tools and human-AI collaboration: it reports a mixed-design study with 42 participants and an offline ablation, claiming fewer corrective edits and reduced physical demand, while retaining geometrically resilient, profile-aligned layouts. These are claims from the abstract; assessing their evidence and limitations would require the full paper.

item.title: Relative Transitions, Not Absolute Destinations: A Transfer-and-Ground Framework for Target-Trajectory-Free Human Mobility Generation
item.summary: Individual mobility trajectories support urban analysis and location-based services, yet most trajectory generators require observations from their deployment city. This assumption excludes precisely the cities where trajectories are unavailable even though points of interest (POIs) and their attributes can be obtained from public maps. We study target-trajectory-free generation: learning from POIs and trajectories in source cities while utilizing only POI coordinates and categories in a target city, with no target trajectory or trajectory-derived statistic available for training, model selection, or generation. Existing trajectory generators typically predict absolute destinations, entangling reusable movement behavior with city-specific POI identities and spatial layouts. Our core insight is to replace this city-bound output with context-conditioned relative transitions. We propose Nomad, a transfer-and-ground framework that separates learning how people move from determining where those movements are realized. Specifically, a history-conditioned flow-matching model learns from source trajectories a transition prior over semantic displacement between POI contexts, geographic displacement, and elapsed time; at inference, a behavior graph and an exploration--return walk ground sampled transitions onto the target POI map. This factorization enables a direct test of representation level transferability without assuming invariance of the full mobility distribution. Extensive experiments across ten cities and 14 transfers show that Nomad outperforms adaptation baselines in trajectory fidelity and downstream utility, lowering the average error over the best baseline of each metric by about 15% in distributional fidelity and about 3% in downstream utility.

items.context: Points of interest (POIs) are mapped locations with attributes such as categories. Mobility trajectories record sequences of visits and movements. This abstract describes a setting where a model learns movement patterns from source cities but has access only to POI coordinates and categories—not trajectories or trajectory-derived statistics—in a target city. It contrasts predicting absolute destinations with modeling relative transitions conditioned on POI context, geographic displacement, and elapsed time; these are concepts in the proposed approach, not established guarantees of transferability.
items.why: The abstract is useful for readers interested in generating mobility trajectories when target-city trajectory data is unavailable. It outlines Nomad’s separation of learned movement behavior from mapping that behavior onto a target city’s POIs, and reports tests across ten cities and 14 transfers. The authors report better trajectory fidelity than adaptation baselines and improvements in downstream utility, while the abstract alone does not provide the full experimental details.
